promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Nov 1 2026, 8 weeks out, target under 3:45.

new.headline: Do not make up the missed miles: last week's shortfall came from heat and 5.5-hour nights, not lost fitness. Next week is a planned lighter 29 miles with one short quality session and a 10-mile long run.

flags.title: Sessions cut short
flags.detail: Wednesday stopped after 2 of 3 reps, Thursday was missed, and the long run ended at 11 of 13 miles. Stopping was the right call in that heat, so nothing gets added back.

flags.title: Heart rate running high
flags.detail: Easy runs sat near 150 bpm at 10:30 pace, against 138 at 9:50 in early August. Judge easy days by effort and being able to talk until the weather cools.

flags.title: Sleep and stress
flags.detail: You averaged 5.5 hours with a work deadline and a hot apartment. Right now sleep limits your training more than mileage does.

flags.title: Right knee
flags.detail: It was quiet all week, but it flared in mid-August on downhills. Tell me if the outside of the knee tightens early in a run, and restart the hip and glute work you skipped last week.

flags.title: Long run progress
flags.detail: At 11 miles in heat, the long run is behind where it needs to be with about 8 weeks to go. The climb restarts the week of Sep 7 – 13 if sleep and heart rate recover.

answers.question: I missed Thursday and cut the long run short. Should I make up the miles next week?
answers.answer:
No, leave the missed miles behind. About 9 miles went missing against the plan, and they went because of heat, a hot apartment and short nights. Packing them into next week would dig the hole deeper.

One short week does not cost you fitness. Adding miles to a drained body is how the knee trouble from mid-August could come back. Next week is a planned lighter 29 miles instead, and the long run starts climbing again the week of Sep 7 – 13 if you recover.

new.analysis:
## Heat and sleep, not lost fitness

Last week was a heat-and-sleep problem rather than a fitness problem. Your body worked harder for every mile at slower paces, which is what hot nights and 5.5 hours of sleep do. One week does not erase the 12-mile long run and the 8:00 threshold reps you handled earlier in August.

| Run | Pace | Avg heart rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Easy runs, early to mid August | 9:50/mi | 138–139 bpm |
| Easy run, Tue Aug 25 | 10:24/mi | 153 bpm |
| Easy run, Sat Aug 29 | 10:34/mi | 149 bpm |
| Long run, Sun Aug 23 | 10:02/mi | 146 bpm |
| Long run, Sun Aug 30 | 10:35/mi while moving | 156 bpm |

The two sessions that mattered most ran harder than intended. The threshold session ended at effort 9/10 against a planned 7, and the long run at 8/10 with 17% of it in zone 4 when it was meant to be easy. That is also why your easy-running share fell to 10.8%: heat pushed heart rate into zone 3 at easy pace, so the number reflects conditions more than poor discipline.

## Why a lighter week now

A lighter week is due anyway. You have had five build weeks with no planned step back, and the last two were already trimmed by the knee and then the heat. A deliberate 29 miles costs little and should leave you fresher for the climb that follows.

About eight weeks is still enough time. A 3:45 finish means roughly 8:35/mi, which is slower than the threshold pace you held in early August, so the engine is there. What is behind is the long run, which should build toward 2.5 to 3 hours, roughly 15 to 18 miles at your easy pace. Marathon-pace segments go into the long run once you are recovered, not this week.

## Conditions for the week

The quality session comes with a condition. Do it only after a night of at least 6 hours and in cool conditions, otherwise swap it for easy running and move on. If easy-run heart rate in cooler weather is still 10 bpm above your early-August level after a few better nights, tell me and I will cut the following week back rather than push through.

Strength fell to 0 of 2 last week after four sessions the week before. With the knee flare still recent, ten minutes of hip and glute work after an easy run is cheaper than a separate session. It also protects the one thing that cost you a long run in mid-August.

The apartment is the other lever. A fan, a cool shower and lights out earlier will do more for you this week than any extra mile.

settingsProposalBullets: Add that the outside of your right knee flared in mid-August (up to 4/10 on downhills) and settled by Aug 23, since "no injuries in the last two years" is now out of date.
Use 9:50/mi at about 138 bpm as your cool-weather easy baseline, so I can tell heat days from fitness changes.
Add hip and glute strength work, twice a week, to what I know about you.
Note that your apartment is too hot to sleep until the AC is fixed, so I plan around sleep until you tell me it is sorted.

safetyCallouts.title: Heat and tiredness.
safetyCallouts.body: Run in the coolest hours, carry water, and stop and get help if you feel dizzy or unwell. If you still feel drained after a week of better sleep, mention it to your doctor.
